subject: computer-science
title: Databases: The Relational Model
welcome_lead: Tables, keys and relationships — the backbone of every business system.
meta_desc: A-Level CS: relations, primary and foreign keys, entity-relationship.
final_note: Get the model right and the queries follow.

concepts.def: In the relational model, a table: a set of tuples (rows) sharing the same attributes (columns), each describing one entity instance.
An attribute or minimal set of attributes that uniquely identifies each row in a table; no two rows may share its value.
The SQL statement that retrieves data, naming the columns wanted, the table to query and optional conditions, ordering and grouping.
The part of an SQL statement that filters rows, keeping only those for which the stated condition evaluates to true.
An SQL operation combining rows from two tables by matching values, typically pairing a foreign key with the primary key it references.
SQL functions such as COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX that compute a single summary value over a set of rows.

walkthroughs.body_html: The relational model (Codd, 1970) represents data as relations — sets of tuples with named attributes. Operations come from relational algebra (select, project, join).
A primary key uniquely identifies a row. A foreign key in one table references the primary key of another, enforcing referential integrity.
An ER diagram shows entities (boxes), attributes (ovals) and relationships (diamonds). Cardinality is annotated as 1:1, 1:M or M:N. M:N relationships need a junction table.

mcqs.q: Which SQL keyword filters rows according to a condition?
options: WHERE
ORDER
FROM
INTO

mcqs.q: An SQL JOIN is used to:
options: Combine rows from two tables by matching key values
Delete two tables at once
Rename the database
Create a user account

mcqs.q: COUNT, SUM and AVG are examples of:
options: Aggregate functions that summarise many rows into one value
Data types
Primary keys
Network protocols

mcqs.q: What is the difference between DELETE and DROP TABLE?
options: DELETE removes rows from a table; DROP TABLE removes the entire table and its structure
They do exactly the same thing
DELETE removes the whole database
DROP TABLE only removes one row

mcqs.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING in SQL?
options: Yes - DELETE also removes the whole database file.
HAVING is just the British spelling of WHERE.
WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping; HAVING filters the groups produced by GROUP BY, typically using aggregate values.
They are interchangeable - both filter rows at any point.

mcqs.q: Does DELETE FROM Students remove the Students table?
options: Yes - DELETE also removes the whole database file.
Yes - DELETE and DROP both erase the table completely.
HAVING is just the British spelling of WHERE.
No - DELETE removes rows (all of them, without a WHERE clause) but the empty table and its structure remain; DROP TABLE removes the table itself.

mcqs.q: Is SELECT * the required way to start every query?
options: No - the asterisk is shorthand for all columns; naming only the columns you need is usually better practice, reducing transferred data and ambiguity.
Yes - SQL syntax demands the asterisk in every SELECT.
Yes - SELECT without * returns no data at all.
HAVING is just the British spelling of WHERE.
